theme: The purpose of Proverbs; wisdom’s call; the two paths
readingInstruction: Read Proverbs 1:1-2:22. These chapters introduce the whole book. Read the opening statement of purpose slowly, then listen to the voice of Wisdom crying out in the street.
settingTheScene: Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings, largely associated with Solomon, gathered over generations in Israel. It is not a book of promises or laws. It is practical instruction on how to live well in God’s world, written mostly as a father speaking to his son. The first nine chapters form an extended introduction, urging the reader to choose wisdom over folly. You have just read the story of Solomon, who asked for wisdom and then lost his way. Now you read the wisdom itself.
observation: The book is for “learning about wisdom and instruction, for understanding words of insight” (1:2).
“The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge; fools despise wisdom and instruction” (1:7).
“Hear, my son, your father’s instruction, and forsake not your mother’s teaching” (1:8).
Sinners entice: “Come with us… let us ambush the blameless” (1:10-19).
“Wisdom cries aloud in the street, in the markets she raises her voice” (1:20).
“Whoever listens to me will dwell secure and will be at ease, without dread of disaster” (1:33).
“For the LORD gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding” (2:6).
Wisdom will deliver “from the way of evil” and “from the forbidden woman” (2:12, 16).
interpretation:
The opening sentence of Proverbs sets the agenda. This is a book about skill in living: how to handle money, words, friendships, work, sex, and anger in a way that fits the world as God made it. The Hebrew word for wisdom means practical skill, like the skill of a craftsman. Wisdom is not first about being clever. It is about being rightly aligned.

Verse 7 is the key to the whole book: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge.” To fear the LORD is to take him seriously as God, to live in reverent awe and trust before him. It is not terror but a right orientation. Everything else in the book flows from it. A person can be intelligent and still be a fool if he leaves God out. The beginning point of wisdom is not information, but a relationship.

The book is delivered as a father’s teaching, and the father warns his son about the pull of the crowd. The sinners’ invitation is attractive: easy money and belonging. But Proverbs says the gang is heading for a trap, “lying in wait for their own blood.” The hardest part of the lesson is that sin often looks like a shortcut.

Wisdom is then personified as a woman crying aloud in the street. She is not hidden. She calls in the markets and at the gates. The tragedy is that people do not listen. When disaster comes, she says, “I will laugh at your calamity,” meaning that those who refused every invitation are left to what they chose. But those who listen “will dwell secure.”

Chapter 2 gives the path to wisdom: receive the words, treasure the commands, call out for insight, and seek it like silver. And it gives the source: “The LORD gives wisdom.” We do not find wisdom by ourselves. We ask for it, and God gives it. The chapter ends with two ways: the path of the upright, who will dwell in the land, and the way of the wicked, who will be cut off.
connection: Paul says that Christ became to us “wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30), and that in him “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). James 1:5 invites us to ask God for wisdom. Jesus himself taught in the manner of the wise, with parables and sayings, and said the wise man builds on the rock (Matthew 7:24).
application:
Ask God for wisdom today, as the passage urges. Name one decision where you need it.

Think about the voices that invite you to take a shortcut. Which one is loudest right now?

Treat the fear of the LORD as a starting point and not an extra.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to begin wisdom in you by the fear of him.
Ask him to keep you from the way of the crowd.
Tell him where you most need wisdom this week.
